new_camps.name: Barclay Lake bivy
new_camps.why: Only 2.2 trail miles in, with water at the door and flat established sites; you start the brush-bash to the north face from here at first light.
new_camps.capacity: Established sites around the lake; the area takes large groups.
new_camps.notes: The lake sits right under the north face, so the approach next morning is short. The footlog over Barclay Creek was removed as of 2026, so expect a creek crossing on the way in.

camps.name: Dolomite Camp
camps.why: Perched above the first step, it is the camp parties haul to and sleep at on the face, with a snow patch for water and a short push to the upper steps.

camps.name: Couloir Camp
camps.why: A forested staging ledge about 1,000 ft above the lake; most parties pass through it to Dolomite Camp, using it only to split loads or sit out a bad day.

camps.name: Barclay Lake
camps.why: Comfortable lakeside sites at the trailhead end of the approach; it adds a long brush-bash to day one, so it suits only a slow party or a retreat.

plan_conflict: The plan puts the bivy atop the crux step, but the only documented camp on the face is Dolomite Camp at the top of the first step; Couloir Camp and Barclay Lake were both marked main and are now route (they are not slept at on a two-day plan).

camps.name: Chetwoot Lake
camps.why: Quiet flat sites near the outlet, and the climb starts right from camp; it is a long, slow off-trail day to reach but you have the lake mostly to yourself.

camps.name: Big Heart Lake
camps.why: The last maintained-trail camp and a shorter first day, but busy with tents and it leaves the slow cross-country leg to Chetwoot for the morning.

camps.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
camps.why: The usual first-night camp: lakeside sites at the end of the long trail, with the final steep scramble to La Bohn Gap still ahead the next morning.

camps.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
camps.why: Higher and roughly 1,000 ft closer to the gap, so the summit morning is shorter, but it adds a steep, loose, slow haul with a full pack on day one.

camps.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
camps.why: Car-camping the night before gives a pre-dawn start on an 8-mile, 3,200 ft walk-in day; nothing in the valley itself is slept at on the climb.

plan_conflict: Both Necklace Valley and La Bohn Lakes were marked main; Jade Lake is where most parties sleep on a one-night plan, so La Bohn Lakes is now route.

camps.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
camps.why: A short 4-mile walk in, water at the lake, and the gully approach starts within a couple of hours; parties camp here to start before dawn and avoid sun on the gully.

plan_conflict: On file as a route option, but it is the only camp on this plan's one night, so it is now main.

camps.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
camps.why: A flat crest spot with snow nearby for water, and about half the traverse done; the descent from Main then finishes the next day.

camps.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
camps.why: A lower, comfortable bivy the night before the North Face; used on a three-day version that splits the first climb from the high bivy.

plan_conflict: The plan says to bivy on North Peak, but most parties sleep on the crest of Middle Peak (one party slept on the North summit).

camps.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
camps.why: Easy walk-in, water at the lake and a ground base to haul from; the first ascent team returned here after their first day on the wall.

camps.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
camps.why: Portaledge camps are the only way to sleep on a wall this steep; they save descending each day but need a full haul load and water carried.

plan_conflict: The plan lists several days as day 2 and shows three nights; the first ascent took about five nights on the wall after one night at the base, so a repeat is likely shorter but not confirmed.

new_camps.name: Pitch 10 ledge, Bluebell
new_camps.why: The ledge at the top of pitch 10 has extra bolts for portaledges, which splits the route in half; the ledge above pitch 12 is a poor, narrow spot for one.
new_camps.capacity: A portaledge fits; the ledge alone sleeps one poorly.
new_camps.notes: Not every party sleeps on the route; the first-ascent party took two days and some climb it in one. Elevation not found in any source.

new_camps.name: Lake Serene bivy
new_camps.why: A 3.6-mile walk-in puts you at water and below the face for a pre-dawn start; the flat ground north of the lake is brushy, so arrive in daylight.
new_camps.notes: One 2025 party arrived after dark and found the north shore very brushy. The talus basin below the route is the alternative.

new_camps.name: Saddle camp between Wing Peak and Tailgunner (Tailgunner Pass)
new_camps.why: The ridge saddle puts Wing Peak a short walk from the tent; the price is a steep 3,000 ft carry and no water on the saddle in summer.
new_camps.notes: Winter parties have dug a tent platform here and gathered snow. Barclay Creek near the trailhead is the lower water source.

new_camps.name: Camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge
new_camps.why: About an hour from the slab base along the old Shovel Creek track, which makes this the standard camp for the Mega Slab climbs.
new_camps.notes: One party camped at an abandoned trail near Shovel Creek instead, and carried river shoes for the Waptus crossing. Elevation was not found in any source.

new_camps.name: Dutch Miller Gap camp
new_camps.why: The standard night after a long 15-mile walk-in, with established sites and ponds at the gap, leaving a six-hour summit day with a night's rest.
new_camps.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead.
new_camps.notes: Gap elevation is about 5,000 ft; sites sit at or just below it.

new_camps.name: Tarns below the Southwest Face, about 5,300 ft
new_camps.why: Moving up from the gap shortens the summit morning, at the cost of carrying packs another uphill mile past the gap.
new_camps.notes: Used by a 2020 party who moved camp from the gap the same evening.

new_camps.name: Camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge
new_camps.why: About an hour from the slab base along the old Shovel Creek track, which makes this the standard camp for the Mega Slab climbs.
new_camps.notes: One party camped at an abandoned trail near Shovel Creek instead, and carried river shoes for the Waptus crossing. Elevation was not found in any source.

camps.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
camps.why: Flat dirt sites at the high lake put you about 2,000 ft below the summit with water at camp; lower lake has fewer flat sites.

camps.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
camps.why: A lower camp that splits the 7-mile road walk into two shorter days, but it adds a long, steep climb to the lakes before the summit day.

camps.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
camps.why: An established site near the river ford; the summit day starts right across the water, so you leave the packs in camp and the walk-out stays easy.

camps.name: Peggy's Pond — standard base camp and water source
camps.why: Many flat sites near the pond, water at camp, and the couloir starts a short walk away; the exposed path to it makes arriving in daylight important.

new_camps.name: Cathedral Pass camp
new_camps.why: Flat tent sites near the last tarn, about 4 miles in, put you closest to the face; camp away from the water to dodge mosquitoes.
new_camps.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register.
new_camps.notes: A 2025 party planning to go on to Peggy's Pond stopped here and found several flat sites above the tarn.

new_camps.name: Nosh Nosh Wahtum camp
new_camps.why: Lakeside camp 2.5 miles in for a shorter first day, but 1,000 ft lower and farther from the chimney in the morning.
